questions.question: During a TLS handshake, the client encrypts the session key with the server's public key so only the private-key holder can recover it; the algorithm's security rests on the difficulty of factoring large primes. Which algorithm is this?
questions.explanation: Public-key encryption of a session key whose hardness comes from integer factorization is RSA; Diffie-Hellman only derives a shared secret, and ECC relies on discrete logarithms rather than factoring.

questions.question: A VPN gateway must bulk-encrypt traffic quickly using a 128-bit-block symmetric cipher chosen to succeed DES and 3DES. Which standard should it use?
questions.explanation: DES's 56-bit key is breakable and 3DES is slow; the NIST-selected successor for fast symmetric bulk encryption on 128-bit blocks is AES, built on the Rijndael cipher.

questions.question: A site-to-site VPN must authenticate and encrypt entire IP packets between gateways regardless of which application protocol flows inside - protection applied below the transport layer. Which suite provides this?
questions.explanation: TLS protects specific application sessions at layer 4+; securing whole IP packets transparently at Layer 3 with AH/ESP is what IPSec does, which is why site-to-site VPNs use it.

questions.question: A download site publishes a 64-hex-character digest for each file; the user recomputes the value locally and a match proves the file was not altered in transit. Which integrity technique is this?
questions.explanation: A fixed-size fingerprint recomputed from the received data that changes on any tampering is a cryptographic hash (message digest) - encryption would need keys and a signature would need the private key.

questions.question: A firmware image is signed with the vendor's private key, and each device verifies it with the public key - proving both who published it and that it was not modified. Which mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: Signing a hash of the data with a private key that anyone can verify with the public key gives authenticity plus integrity plus non-repudiation - the definition of a digital signature.

questions.question: A browser trusts example.com's certificate because a chain of issuers leads back to a trusted root CA; issuing, distributing, revoking, and validating those certificates depends on which framework?
questions.explanation: Certificate authorities, chains of trust, revocation lists, and the policies binding keys to identities together form the Public Key Infrastructure.

questions.question: Attackers exploited a flaw the very morning it was discovered; no vendor patch and no IDS signature existed yet. What kind of attack is this?
questions.explanation: Exploiting a vulnerability before the vendor or defenders have had a single day to fix or detect it is a zero-day attack; known-CVE exploits and phishing do not fit.

questions.question: A company contracts a red team to safely break into its own systems under agreed rules of engagement and then report every exploitable path found. Which security assessment is this?
questions.explanation: Authorized, simulated real-world attacks that attempt to exploit weaknesses - beyond a mere vulnerability scan's inventory - is penetration testing (ethical hacking).

questions.question: A federal agency structures its security program around the Identify-Protect-Detect-Respond-Recover functions of a cybersecurity framework issued by a US standards body. Which organization published that framework?
alternatives: National Institute of Standards and Technology
questions.explanation: The five core functions Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover belong to the Cybersecurity Framework published by NIST, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology.

questions.question: An email gateway detonates suspicious attachments inside an instrumented virtual machine cut off from production before deciding whether to deliver them. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Running untrusted code in an isolated, instrumented environment to observe its behavior safely is sandboxing; signatures and heuristics inspect the file without executing it.

questions.question: Two parties each choose a private exponent, exchange g^x mod p values over a tapped line, and both compute the same session secret - which itself never crosses the wire. Which key-exchange protocol is this?
questions.explanation: Modular-exponentiation key agreement where each side mixes the other's public value with its private exponent to reach a shared secret, safe from eavesdroppers, is Diffie-Hellman.

questions.question: A certificate's fingerprint field shows a 64-hex-character digest from the SHA-2 family. Which hash algorithm produced it?
questions.explanation: 64 hex characters encode 256 bits (64 x 4 bits); within SHA-2, the member producing a 256-bit digest is SHA-256.

questions.question: To sniff a switched LAN, an attacker injects frames from thousands of fake source addresses until the switch forgets legitimate entries and floods all traffic out every port. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: Exhausting the finite CAM/MAC table with spoofed source addresses forces the switch into fail-open flooding, turning it into a hub so the attacker sees all traffic - that is MAC flooding.

questions.question: After receiving unsolicited gratuitous replies, hosts on a LAN now map the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC and send all their upstream traffic through the attacker's machine. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: Forged ARP replies rewrite victims' ARP caches so a legitimate IP resolves to the attacker's MAC - ARP cache poisoning/spoofing, the classic prelude to a LAN man-in-the-middle.

questions.question: A redesign deletes the trusted internal zone entirely: every request - even one originating inside the LAN - must be authenticated, authorized, and encrypted. Which security model is this?
questions.explanation: Removing implicit trust based on network location and continuously verifying every request is the 'never trust, always verify' principle of the zero trust model.

questions.question: An attacker on a public Wi-Fi network secretly relays and alters messages between a victim and their bank by presenting a forged certificate. What attack is this?
questions.explanation: In a man-in-the-middle attack the adversary interposes between two parties, intercepting and potentially modifying traffic while each side believes it is talking to the other.

questions.question: An attacker sends forged responses to a DNS resolver so that users typing the bank's domain are sent to a malicious IP, and the bad entry is stored. What attack is this?
questions.explanation: DNS cache poisoning injects forged records into a resolver's cache so subsequent lookups return attacker-controlled addresses.

questions.question: A user must enter a password and then approve a push notification on a registered phone before logging in. What is this security mechanism called?
questions.explanation: Two-factor authentication combines two factor types - something you know (password) and something you have (the registered device).

questions.question: An attacker generates two different contract documents - one benign, one malicious - that hash to the identical digest, then gets the benign one signed. Which hash-function property failed to prevent this?
questions.explanation: The attacker chose both inputs freely and found two with the same digest - a collision. Collision resistance is what makes finding any such pair infeasible; second-preimage resistance instead covers finding a match for one given input.

questions.question: An attacker crafts packets with a forged source address belonging to a trusted host so a packet-filtering router accepts them. What technique is being used?
questions.explanation: IP spoofing forges the packet's source address to impersonate a trusted host and bypass address-based filters.
